correctness.rationale: Conjugating the metric equation by V gives [Λ,V†ηV]=0; the simple real spectrum forces a positive diagonal D and every such D works. For B=VD⁻¹ᐟ², η⁻¹=BB† has the same eigenvalues as B†B, and inversion does not change the condition number. An optimum exists in all dimensions: rescale S=D⁻¹ᐟ² so min s_i=1; because G has unit diagonal, κ₂(SGS)≥(max s_i)², making any nonempty bounded sublevel set compact. For a pair, its η-cross term vanishes. After rephasing, the equal squared η-norms of the sum and difference bound 2λ_min(η)(1+c) from above and 2λ_max(η)(1−c) from below, giving the claimed obstruction. At fixed determinant in 2D the scaled Gram trace is minimized uniquely by equal diagonal entries, so D is scalar up to common scale, also when c=0. Its condition number is (1+c)/(1−c), giving the half-angle formula and asymptotic. Sharpness does not assert attainment for an arbitrary higher-dimensional basis; the two-dimensional extremizer can be embedded in an orthogonal direct sum. For n=1 there is no pair bound to apply. The inspected artifacts/verify.py is a bounded real-matrix sanity check and was not executed; the complex and all-dimension claims follow analytically.

evidence: The preconditioning paper treats one-sided positive diagonal column scaling of a general real matrix. Wielandt applies to arbitrary invertible complex matrices and arbitrary transformed angles. The minimally anisotropic paper uses Hilbert–Schmidt distance.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Take A=V in the one-sided scaling problem and square its spectral condition number, obtaining exactly κ₂(D⁻¹ᐟ²GD⁻¹ᐟ²). The inspected preconditioning paper is real; taking the Gram via B†B rather than BᵀB is the direct extension of the identity, not evidence its algorithms were proved there for complex data. The Hilbert–Schmidt objective alone does not determine the spectral-condition optimum.

evidence: The admissible metric set is a positive cone. The earlier two-level result gives d∞(s)=s and a unique nearest positive metric on the equal-normalized-left-projector ray.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: For extreme eigenvalues m,M of η, minimizing ||tη−I||₂ over t>0 balances the two extremes at t=2/(M+m), yielding (M−m)/(M+m). This function is strictly increasing in M/m, so the operator-norm optimum determines the condition optimum and uniqueness up to scale. For two unit right eigenvectors, G⁻¹=(1−c²)⁻¹[[1,−g],[−conj(g),1]], with g their overlap. The columns of V⁻† therefore have equal norm and normalized overlap s=c. Their normalized projector sum is (1−c²)(VV†)⁻¹. Substituting d∞=c gives κ₂=(1+c)/(1−c), the identical minimizing ray, and the angle formula. The remaining claims are the Wielandt specialization and the Gram rewriting of the diagonal-scaling objective.

originality.rationale: The two-level theorem, including optimum value and uniqueness of the ray, follows from the already indexed Schatten-infinity minimization after minimizing over metric scale. The pairwise obstruction is exactly the classical Wielandt inequality for the inverse square root of the metric acting on orthogonal lines. The diagonal-Gram step expresses the standard metric family in the standard one-sided column-scaling objective; it introduces no additional optimizer or estimate.
residual_risks: The limited search does not establish the earliest source for each formulation. Verified coverage suffices for this decision without resolving priority across all matrix-scaling and metric-selection sources.

value.rationale: Optimizing metric conditioning is a meaningful problem, but this record stops at transferring an existing angle inequality and an equivalent known two-level optimization, plus a direct Gram reformulation in higher dimension. As a distinct mathematical finding it supplies neither a new mechanism controlling conditioning nor a new higher-dimensional solution or estimate. It is useful exposition, not a new conditioning theorem under the stated value standard.
